Opinionistas Evidence before the Madlanga Commission illustrates how security companies have become shadow militia, used by criminals to access tenders and guns that they use to intimidate the opposition By Thando Nzimande 24 Aug 2026 Thando Nzimande is a Wits alumnus, a Future Voices scholar and researcher at Meari, a neuroscience researcher and economic and geopolitical commentator/analyst. Dive Deeper Speed Read Listen Dive Deeper Opinion This article is an Opinion , which presents the writer's personal point of view. The views expressed are those of the author/authors and do not necessarily represent the views of Daily Maverick. The Madlanga Commission has pulled back the curtain on a South Africa where the instruments of state power have been repurposed to serve private criminal interests, creating a shadow state that effectively houses multiple private militias boasting more guns and influence than the state police. The prevalence of security company ownership among those implicated in the commissionâs hearings is no accident. It is a direct and inevitable consequence of a system where public funds are looted to build parallel power structures, where the badge and the gun are commodities to be bought and sold and where the private security industry has become the vehicle through which criminal syndicates project force and maintain control. Staggering financial scale of âcriminal enterpriseâ The staggering figures laid bare by the commission illustrate the financial scale of this phenomenon. At the Tshwane Metro Police Department alone, 22 companies were granted a security tender that has seen approximately R2.9-billion paid out to date, with the commission scrutinising allegations of tender manipulation that ensured only a handful of companies remained on the payroll. Among these, Gubis85 Solutions stands out as a particularly egregious example, receiving R59.13-million for ad hoc services between July 2024 and June 2025 on top of its standard monthly security services payment of R3.5-million. The commission heard testimony that the allocation of additional sites to Gubis85 was carried out by junior officials without proper authorisation, with 40 ad hoc sites assigned between January and February 2025 alone, each staffed by 24 security officers and supported by three patrol vehicles. A Tshwane Metro chief later testified that she halted an irregular private security tender costing R800-million that had been approved by a deputy chief. This is not legitimate business; this is the systematic diversion of public resources to build private armies that operate beyond the reach of the law. The question of why these specific people need to arm themselves is answered by the commissionâs findings: it is to maintain control over lucrative tenders, to intimidate rivals and to operate with impunity. The security company is not merely a business venture; it is a franchise of power, a source of revenue, and crucially, a private militia that can be deployed at will. This was made disturbingly clear in the testimony regarding the Ekurhuleni Metropolitan area, where the commission identified a sophisticated criminal syndicate operating within the municipality and the Ekurhuleni Metro Police Department (EMPD). A former EMPD deputy police chief testified that there was a âcriminal enterpriseâ operating within the EMPD, describing a core group of officers who were suspected of serious crimes including murder, robbery, kidnapping and extortion, yet had not been prosecuted or subjected to internal disciplinary processes. Efforts to hold the senior officer leading this group to account were blocked at the highest level of the municipality. The murder of private security officer Marius van der Merwe, who was gunned down outside his home in December 2025 just three weeks after testifying anonymously before the commission, demonstrates the lethal consequences of exposing these networks. Van der Merwe had testified about a night in April 2022 when the group allegedly tortured and killed a robbery suspect in an effort to obtain stolen goods and money for their personal use. His murder appears to have been an act of retribution, intended to silence him and it illustrates the violent power these private security-backed networks wield. Central role of taxi boss Msibi The central figure in this web of private militias and criminal enterprise is the late taxi boss Jothan Msibi , who has been identified by multiple witnesses as the head of the so-called Big Five cartel that infiltrated South African state institutions, politics and the private sector. Msibi, who died in January 2024, was described by a senior policeman as heading a sprawling criminal network that reached into every corner of law enforcement. His funeral was attended by a former police minister, underscoring the political connections that shielded this enterprise. Msibi was identified as the owner of security company Themy Styles, while his associate Katiso Molefe, a man accused of orchestrating several contract killings, was listed as its director. The ownership of this security company was not incidental to Msibiâs operations; it was central to his ability to project force and control the various criminal enterprises he was involved in. The commission has uncovered evidence that Msibiâs security company and his network were involved in a breathtaking array of criminal activities. WhatsApp messages presented at the inquiry revealed that Carnilinx, a controversial tobacco company, used Msibi to retrieve stolen stock and firearms. In one exchange, Carnilinx director Kyle Phillips messaged Msibi, addressing him as âPappa Joeâ and thanking him for sorting out a theft, asking if the firearms could also be recovered. This demonstrates that Msibiâs private security apparatus was being deployed not just for conventional security work but as an enforcement arm for criminal enterprises. In another exchange, Phillips offered Msibi âred waterâ, a substance associated with illicit gold processing, further cementing the connection between the security company and organised crime. Alleged plot to acquire spy equipment Perhaps most alarmingly, the commission has exposed an alleged plot involving Msibi, suspended Sergeant Fannie Nkosi, Molefe and private security businessman Steve Motsumi to acquire sophisticated phone-interception technology known as âgrabbersâ from a Czech Republic-based company for resale in Eswatini. The evidence suggests that Nkosi used a police stamp and his force number on a procurement document to help advance the deal, effectively using the stateâs authority as a front for a private transaction. WhatsApp exchanges presented to the commission provided a glimpse into the negotiations, with Nkosi forwarding a message from a contact asking whether the âSwazi dealâ remained possible, and Msibi replying: âItâs on the table but they have to display. We donât want to become fools.â The evidence leader told the commission that it was âvery worryingâ that members of the alleged cartel were claiming to be representatives of the state and engaging with foreign companies about spy tools that should only be in the hands of intelligence agencies operating under strict regulations. This is not a private security company in any legitimate sense; this is a criminal syndicate masquerading as a commercial enterprise, using state resources and authority to trade in surveillance technology that could be used against citizens. Msibiâs influence was not limited to the underworld. The commission has also linked him to alleged tender fraud at the Ekurhuleni Municipality. WhatsApp messages revealed Msibiâs alleged involvement in rigging a tender for a project management unit at the municipality, where he personally nominated a company called Camp Rock for the bid. The tender was subsequently awarded to Camp Rock, a company tied to an associate of Msibi, demonstrating how the security company owner could manipulate state procurement processes for private benefit. The connections emanating from Msibi reach further into the political sphere, with his phone records showing he communicated with former Ekurhuleni city manager Imogen Mashazi. Alleged crime boss Matlala reflects same pattern The figure of Vusimuzi âCatâ Matlala , an alleged crime boss who has been described as a leader within the Big Five cartel, further illustrates this pattern. The commission has heard that Matlalaâs company Cat VIP Security had an âunlawfulâ agreement with the EMPD to supply surveillance technology, suspect-tracking tools and tactical support in pursuing violent repeat offenders. A former EMPD deputy chief testified that a memorandum of understanding signed by a suspended brigadier unlawfully granted the private security firm access to EMPD surveillance systems and effectively outsourced core policing duties to a private company, leaving EMPD operations hollow and insufficient. Matlala, however, told the commission that none of his companies was ever awarded contracts by the EMPD, stating that the only business he conducted was for no financial gain when his company provided security services to a former mayor. He claimed privilege against self-incrimination regarding his pending trial over the Medicare 24 Tshwane contract with the South African Police Services (SAPS). State security captured from within What the Madlanga Commission has revealed is a country where the state has effectively been captured from within, where law enforcement resources have been repurposed to serve criminal interests and where private security companies have become the vehicle for this criminal capture. The individuals implicated in the Madlanga inquiry own security companies because they need to arm themselves against rivals and law enforcement, yes â but also because they need to maintain control over their criminal enterprises. The security company provides them with the legitimacy to employ armed personnel, the financial vehicle to launder money and the operational cover to conduct illegal activities. As the commission continues its work, the revelation that South Africa is housing multiple private militias that rival the state police in firepower and influence stands as one of the most disturbing findings to emerge from this inquiry. The path to reform will require not just prosecuting the individuals involved but dismantling the entire system that has allowed private security to become a tool of criminal enterprise. Photograph: Evan Simon / Floodlight View image in fullscreen One of the largest data centers on the East Coast, DataOne is the first in New Jersey seeking to build its own power plant. Photograph: Evan Simon / Floodlight Floodlight Pollution US datacenter discharged large amounts of pollution for almost a year with no permits Records show Vineland facility in New Jersey emitted health-harming pollution before regulators stepped in Evan Simon of Floodlight Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google DataOne, the Microsoft-linked New Jersey datacenter recently hit with a $1m fine for running unpermitted generators, emitted large amounts of health-harming air pollution for nearly a year before state regulators stepped in, according to public records obtained by Floodlight. The Vineland facility’s 62 gas-fired generators became public in August after a Floodlight/Guardian visual investigation found them operating without permits. The New Jersey department of environmental protection last week fined the company over the fleet but did not disclose how long the generators had been operating nor how much air pollution they had released into the surrounding community over the past year. Floodlight sent technical data about the generators – obtained through public records requests – to a Rutgers professor and a former EPA air division chief. “Our best estimate is that the generators emitted about 140 tons of NOx,” said Xiaomeng Jin, an assistant professor at Rutgers department of environmental sciences. Her analysis would rank DataOne in the state’s top five NOx polluters of 2025, per EPA data. NOx are a dangerous group of smog-producing gases linked to asthma , heart attacks and even premature death . It’s “the most important air pollutant in the US that affects most people”, Jin said. Longtime Vineland resident Tiffany Leone-Vespa lives about a mile from the data center and said the noise from the generators sounds like an airplane in the back of her house. “What health problems might I face in the future? Because I’ve been exposed to all of that. My kids have been exposed to it,” she said. The site’s potential NOx emissions are even larger, according to Jin and Bruce Buckheit – a former EPA air enforcement division chief. Both concluded that at full use, DataOne’s fleet could emit more than 1,500 tons of NOx per year. That is nearly twice the amount that the Linden Cogeneration gas-fired power plant, New Jersey’s largest NOx emitter, is allowed to emit. Operating the generators “results in very high levels of air pollution” and the fleet’s potential emissions are “well over the regulatory threshold for a new major source”, said Buckheit. New Jersey labels any facility capable of emitting more than 25 tons of NOx per year a “major source”. Obtaining a major source permit requires extensive environmental reviews, best available pollution controls and public comment periods – all before construction can even begin. That didn’t happen at DataOne, despite the operation being capable of emitting more than half the NOx put out by New Jersey’s entire power sector. Drone video shows heat signature of datacenter generators “That is basically offsetting all the air quality improvements [regulators] have achieved for decades,” Jin said. DataOne did not respond to Floodlight’s emissions analysis. Instead, its spokesperson sent the same statement as they did in response to NJDEP’s decision to fine them, saying the company is “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells as part of the site’s permanent power solution and have the necessary approvals in place for this solution”. The company disagrees with NJDEP’s determination and had argued the generators did not require permits – but plans to apply for them now. A Microsoft spokesperson wrote that “we expect our suppliers and partners to meet all applicable legal and regulatory obligations” and the company was working with DataOne “to support their completion of the facility’s transition to its permanent long-term power solution”. In press releases, New Jersey regulators said the tractor-trailer-sized generators were detected during a July 29, 2026, site inspection but not during an earlier visit in December. However, the fleet was there to find, according to a letter DataOne later sent NJDEP. The letter, obtained by Floodlight through a public records request, notes the generators first began to arrive in July 2025. Sixteen generators started operating in October 2025, with another 16 brought online in early February. By June, all 62 had been fired up. By the time state inspectors noticed them, the unpermitted fleet had collectively run for more than 46,000 hours in total, according to the letter. “How did 62 generators get installed and operated and nobody did anything until now? That blows me away,” Leone-Vespa said. “Clearly somebody wasn’t doing their job.” A spokesperson for NJDEP declined to comment. For many Vineland residents, confirmation that DataOne’s generators have been running for nearly a year is a bittersweet vindication. Locals have reported strange noises emanating from the facility for months, with more than 100 noise complaints submitted to the Cumberland county department of health since March, according to records obtained by Floodlight. Many of the complaints list generators as the suspected source. “They’re just running these monster generators. And they think, by right, they have every ability to do so at the expense of anyone else,” said local flower farmer Michael Atkinson. Atkinson’s family has been farming a patch of land beside the data center for more than 70 years. He said DataOne is “one of the richest and worst neighbors that I have ever had to deal with in my entire life”. During a Vineland town hall meeting in late January , DataOne chief executive Charles Beyney told residents that his data center would be “polluting less than a farm”. “I’m too French to just kill my lungs, the lungs of your kids and all the community around us,” he told the crowd. Beyney confirmed during that speech that DataOne was running generators, and he said NJDEP was aware – the agency had been at the site that same morning and was “on us big time”. While the generators may have evaded state regulators for almost a year, local officials knew about them for much longer. A City of Vineland inspection activity report noted that “phase 1 generators are online” in early February. And in May, a Cumberland county health department inspector responding to a noise complaint visited the site and reported that the source of the noise appeared to be two generators, “possibly more”. The inspector noted that the noise “exceeded night-time violation”. As part of the record fine levied against DataOne, the state is mandating the company apply for and obtain the required permits or cease operations, but is allowing them 45 days to do so, according to a NJDEP spokesperson. During that time, regulators are allowing the facility to continue running the generators – which are capable of emitting more than four tons of NOx in nearby neighborhoods each day. “I just don’t understand how this is being allowed,” Leone-Vespa said. She hopes independent air monitoring can help protect her community in the future. Until then, she has little faith in New Jersey regulators to watch out for them. “It’s like they don’t care about the residents. This story is from Floodlight , a non-profit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. https://www.politico.eu/article/ukrainia.text: Ukraine’s strikes on data centers inside Russia aimed to disrupt military planning and communication services. There were also reports of another kind of disruption: to customers waiting for their dinner from food-delivery apps. Kyiv’s drone strikes on three Yandex data centers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir saw delays and interruptions for thousands of businesses and households that rely on Yandex's cloud infrastructure, including e-commerce, digital payment platforms and apps of food delivery and car services. Ukrainian drones on Wednesday targeted a major Sberbank data center in Russia’s Saratov region, though a senior company executive said it hadn’t affected operations. After the strikes on Russian data centers, Kyiv noted that Moscow has already repeatedly targeted its digital infrastructure. “Ukrainians wanted to show Russians that two can play this game,” a senior official familiar with the operation told POLITICO, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. Advertisement Advertisement The attacks and counter-attacks point to a new frontline in war: the infrastructure powering the digital economy. The attacks on the buildings that supply compute power are akin to striking a power plant supplying the electricity, heating and fuel that both militaries and civilians depend on. It may weaken an enemy's war effort but can also bring everyday life to a standstill. Experts say the cost of rebuilding in Russia will be particularly high as the centers require scarce materials that must be imported. “Obtaining a large amount of equipment to replace what was destroyed is not going to be easy,” said Oleg Shakirov, a cyber policy and international security researcher, noting that most hardware needs to be imported and that is complicated by high global demand and sanctions on Russia. “To be honest, no one really knows what’s the actual damage. Since two data centers are still offline, we can assume that it’s significant,” said Shakirov. Joseph Jarnacki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that normalizing strikes to data centers could have a new set of dangerous consequences. “These strikes likely breach International Humanitarian Law and it’s a big risk when global populations increasingly rely on digital services,” he told POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement When servers become targets Data centers have entered the crosshairs of other recent armed conflicts. During the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran earlier this year, drone strikes hit three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. Since data centers can serve civilian and military purposes simultaneously, the legal status of targeting them is far from straightforward. Kubo Mačák, an expert on international humanitarian law, said a data center must meet two conditions to qualify as a military objective under the Geneva Conventions: it must make an effective contribution to military operations and destroying it must offer a “definite military advantage.” A delivery robot from Russian tech giant Yandex moves through Moscow. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images “If you know that they are storing military intelligence or that they're using the data center to power military artificial intelligence tools,” Mačák said, there could be grounds to consider it a military objective. Following the most recent strikes of the Yandex data centers, users on social media platform X reported a sudden drop in automated bot activity, including from accounts associated with pro-Russian, pro-Trump and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narratives. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seized on the reports to boast that the strikes had made social media less toxic, even as independent researchers and national research institutes found no evidence they specifically disrupted any Russian disinformation campaigns. Advertisement Advertisement Mačák said that even if a data center is being used to “let's say, run some trolls or these bot farms to interfere with elections abroad … that would not be sufficient.” In other words, hosting propaganda bots does not, by itself, make a data center a lawful military target. The dual-use quandary has often focused on the targeting of energy infrastructure, which has been frequent in the Russia-Ukraine war. On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for rising fuel prices. He has since called for both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, although the existence of any ceasefire agreement remains disputed. As data centers become increasingly central to national economies, they will become more consequential targets. A senior NATO official granted anonymity to discuss the matter told POLITICO that data centers are already considered potential targets and that the alliance is factoring their vulnerability into its planning. NATO allies recognize that their data centers could come under attack in a conflict, the official said: “We would get it in a fight.” Veronika Melkozerova in Kyiv contributed to this report.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: Josephine Schneider’s House in Frederiksberg, Denmark. Photograph: Ole Jensen/Ole Jensen/Getty Images for The Guardian View image in fullscreen Josephine Schneider’s House in Frederiksberg, Denmark. Photograph: Ole Jensen/Ole Jensen/Getty Images for The Guardian Children English children’s homes are in crisis. Does Denmark hold the answers? UK children’s minister Josh MacAlister has travelled to Copenhagen to see what can be learned from Danish system Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent Sun 1 Nov 2026 03.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n a quiet suburb on the outskirts of Copenhagen sits a large white house, set back from the road behind a purple-leaved plum tree. It looks much like the rest of the buildings on the street and there is little outward sign this is Josephine Schneider’s House, considered one of the best children’s homes in the world. Danish children’s homes are often cited as the gold standard of children’s residential care globally. They are now being studied by the British government as it tries to create a roadmap out of the crisis in which its own children’s home system has become mired. Last year there were 669 children living in illegal, unregistered children’s homes across England, with councils paying more than £125m of taxpayers’ money to keep them there . Overall spending on children’s homes soared 96% in five years to over £3.1bn in 2023-24, while standards have dropped, private equity firms are cashing in and a growing number of children are being sent to homes hundreds of miles away. The situation is dire, the children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, admits. “We now have this shadow system of unregistered, illegal homes, which is certainly not providing therapeutic support and the costs are huge,” he said. “We need big changes, a major shake up, and I spend as many hours as I can a week on children’s social care reform.” View image in fullscreen Josh MacAlister and Mads Sørensen, deputy director of Josephine Schneider’s House. Photograph: Patricia Glindorf Earlier this week, MacAlister visited Denmark to see how its children’s homes operate and what can be exported back to England, as part of a Department for Education review into how the sector can be improved. The 140-year-old Josephine Schneider’s House , which houses 12 children and young adults aged six to 23, is starkly different from many British equivalents. In the centre of the house is a spacious kitchen staffed by the head chef, Rasmus, who cooks the children’s meals, lunch boxes and after-school snacks – pizza rolls are a particular favourite. He works with the children himself, encouraging them to help make the food and come grocery shopping. The Copenhagen house that’s probably the best children’s home in the world | Clare Considine and Helen Russell Read more The rest of the staff are all degree-level professionals in social pedagogy, a discipline focusing on psychology, child development and ethics, and they strive to recreate a traditional family home by cooking, eating and socialising with the children. “We don’t have an in-house therapist but everything we do is therapeutic,” said Mads Sørensen, deputy director of the home. One member of staff sleeps in the house at night and wakes the children up each day at 7am. “We ask them how they like to be woken up, to help them feel safe and create that predictability, make their nervous system calm a bit,” Sørensen said. Many of the children here have suffered physical, emotional and social neglect, and issues such as self-harm, insomnia and eating disorders are common. Unlike children’s homes in England, where many children report being isolated and cut off from family and friends, here children are encouraged to have friends stay at the weekends and holidays, there are regular parents evenings, including a Christmas banquet. View image in fullscreen In the centre of the house is a spacious kitchen, with the children encouraged to help make the food. Photograph: Ole Jensen/Ole Jensen/Getty Images for The Guardian Each child also has a team of two to three staff members working with them on their education and wellbeing. In a semi-independent flat on the top floor live the older residents, aged 17 and above, who have their own living area and kitchen as they start to transition into adulthood. The young people buy their own food and do their own chores, under the guidance of staff, preparing them for independent life beyond the home. They are allowed to stay in the home up until the age of 23, and encouraged to return for regular visits beyond that age. This is a far cry from children’s homes in England, which teenagers must leave as soon as they turn 18, part of the cliff-edge loss of support that is causing the early deaths of care leavers . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion MacAlister said he may change this. “Getting rid of the really binary date of birth point to decide where you live is something I’m really persuaded by,” he said. “I hear of children being forced to move when they turn 18, even if they’re in the middle of sitting their A-levels. We have to move away from that.” He also wants to import some of the culture from Danish children’s homes, particularly their focus on personal growth and maintaining family relationships. “A lot of residential care in England is actually about adults containing their own anxiety and concerns about teenagers, and that’s a really poor model,” MacAlister said. “The first question is always ‘how do we protect ourselves from risk?’ which is not what we should be asking first. It’s very different here in Denmark.” The quality of staff is crucial, and something at the heart of the ongoing review, which is being led by Emmanuel Akpan-Inwang, the director of Lighthouse Pedagogy Trust, which runs a children’s home in Sutton based on pedagogy principles. “What’s interesting about Denmark is working in a children’s home is a career that people really want to do,” he said. “It’s competitive. Homes are able to select really great people. They support and train them. They stay in the sector for long periods of time. “But we can’t simply lift and shift the system to England. The Danes have spent more than 40 years developing it. But we can learn from it.” At Josephine Schneider’s House, many staff members have been there 10 years or longer. In the UK, about 53% of children’s home staff have worked in the sector for three years or less. Poor pay, working conditions and a lack of training force many to leave the sector early. But underpinning Danish children’s homes is extensive state funding – a third of homes are publicly owned, 42% are not-for-profit and 27% are private profit. By contrast, in England, 83% of children’s homes places are now privately run, with some operators recording profit margins of more than 20%. The government has passed laws giving itself the power to intervene and cap profits by private providers but has yet to use it, with MacAlister saying they need to wait for a new “market oversight body” to provide full transparency of exactly how much money is being made before they can push ahead. The government of Wales is moving more quickly, and will ban all for-profit providers in children’s social care by 2030. But MacAlister said it would not be easy to replicate this in England, where numbers are much bigger. “We need to massively boost local authorities so they can take back control of the whole purchasing process, curb demand by making sure more children can live in foster homes or kinship arrangements, and shape a system on our terms, not one that is driven by profit,” MacAlister said.
